newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour's Blair attacks on sleaze, leadership.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour's Blair attacks on sleaze, leadership.

text.p: British Labour leader Tony Blair on Wednesday stepped up his criticism of Prime Minister John Major for standing by a former Conservative minister embroiled in allegations of sleaze.

At an election rally of Labour supporters in Plymouth, western England, Blair blasted Major for weak leadership in not dumping Neil Hamilton, even though the former trade minister had admitted breaking parliamentary rules by failing to declare gifts and payments.
Hamilton strenuously denies the more serious charge that he accepted bundles of cash from Mohammed al Fayed, owner of London department store Harrods, in return for asking questions in parliament.
Blair said he was willing to give Hamilton the benefit of the doubt on these allegations.

"But there are enough admitted wrongdoings to merit Mr Hamilton's stepping down, and it is a stain on the political process that he has not," Blair said on the final stop of a campaign swing through western England.
"He stands at this election as a symbol of Tory dishonesty and a testimony to weak leadership," he added.
Major, trailing Blair badly in opinion polls, has been trying to deflect attention from character issues by highlighting Britain's economic record.

But sleaze is likely to stay in the headlines after Hamilton's Conservative association in Tatton, northwest England, selected him on Tuesday as their candidate for the May 1 election, triggering a ballot-box showdown with veteran BBC war reporter Martin Bell.
The Labour and minority Liberal Democrat candidates have agreed to step down to give Bell a clear run at Hamilton on a "White Knight" anti-corruption platform.

The Conservative high command put strong pressure on Hamilton at the start of the campaign to stand down. But when he dug in his heels, Major backed off, saying he did not have the power to tell Tatton Conservatives what to do.
Blair, whose taunts of weak leadership have visibly irked Major before, said he would have sacked a Labour candidate who had admitted wrongdoings as serious as Hamilton's.

"Yet he is still there. The fact that he is still there has nothing whatsoever to do with the rules of the Conservative Party constitution and everything to do with the weakness of the Conservative party leadership.
"The whole episode reminds us of the weak leadership that has characterised the last six years," Blair said.
He was introduced at the rally by British actor Patrick Stewart, better known as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the cult science fiction series Star Trek.
Blair couldn't resist a Star Trek pun, telling his audience that the Conservatives were the earthly incarnation of the evil Klingons.
"First we had John Major clinging on as long as he could before he could before calling an election. Now the ultimate Cling-On -- the so-called honourable member for Tatton," he said.
